{{Short description|Authenticated encryption mode for block ciphers}}
'''CCM mode''' ('''counter with cipher block chaining message authentication code'''; '''counter with [[CBC-MAC]]''') is a [[block cipher modes of operation|mode of operation]] for cryptographic [[block cipher]]s.  It is an [[authenticated encryption]] algorithm designed to provide both [[authentication]] and [[confidentiality]].  CCM mode is only defined for block ciphers with a block length of 128 bits.<ref name="NIST SP800-38C">{{cite tech report
| first = Morris
| last = Dworkin
| title = Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: The CCM Mode for Authentication and Confidentiality
| institution = [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|NIST]]
| series = NIST Special Publications
| number = 800-38C
| date = May 2004
| doi = 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-38C
| url = http://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38c.pdf
| doi-access = free
}}</ref><ref name="RFC3610">{{cite IETF
| title = Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM)
| rfc = 3610
| first1 = D.
| last1 = Whiting
| first2 = R.
| last2 = Housley
| first3 = N.
| last3 = Ferguson
| publisher = [[Internet Engineering Task Force|IETF]]
| date=September 2003
}}</ref>

The [[Cryptographic_nonce|nonce]] of CCM must be carefully chosen to never be used more than once for a given [[Key (cryptography)|key]].
This is because CCM is a derivation of [[block cipher modes of operation#Counter .28CTR.29|counter (CTR) mode]] and the latter is effectively a [[stream cipher]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=rfc4309|url=http://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4309#page-3|journal=IETF|date=December 2005 |page=3|quote=AES CCM employs counter mode for encryption.  As with any stream cipher, reuse of the same IV value with the same key is catastrophic. |last1=Housley |first1=Russ }}</ref>

==Encryption and authentication==

As the name suggests, CCM mode combines [[Block cipher modes of operation#Counter .28CTR.29|counter (CTR) mode]] for confidentiality with [[CBC-MAC|cipher block chaining message authentication code (CBC-MAC)]] for authentication. These two primitives are applied in an "authenticate-then-encrypt" manner: CBC-MAC is first computed on the message to obtain a [[Message authentication code|message authentication code (MAC)]], then the message and the MAC are encrypted using counter mode. The main insight is that the same encryption key can be used for both, provided that the counter values used in the encryption do not collide with the (pre-)[[initialization vector]] used in the authentication. A [[Provable_security#In_cryptography|proof of security]]<ref>{{cite book | chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/3-540-36492-7_7.pdf | doi=10.1007/3-540-36492-7_7 | chapter=On the Security of CTR + CBC-MAC | title=Selected Areas in Cryptography | series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science | date=2003 | last1=Jonsson | first1=Jakob | volume=2595 | pages=76–93 | isbn=978-3-540-00622-0 }}</ref> exists for this combination, based on the security of the underlying block cipher. The proof also applies to a generalization of CCM for any [[Block size (cryptography)|block size]], and for any size of [[cryptographically strong]] [[pseudo-random function]] (since in both counter mode and CBC-MAC, the block cipher is only ever used in one direction).

CCM mode was designed by [[Russ Housley]], Doug Whiting and [[Niels Ferguson]].  At the time CCM mode was developed, Russ Housley was employed by [[RSA Security|RSA Laboratories]].

A minor variation of CCM, called CCM*, is used in the [[IEEE 802.15.4]] standard, used as the [[medium access control|MAC]] layer in [[Zigbee]]. CCM* includes all of the features of CCM. It allows a choice of MAC lengths down to 0 (which disables authentication and becomes encryption-only).<ref name=ieee802154>{{cite book|url=https://www.corsi.univr.it/documenti/OccorrenzaIns/matdid/matdid342697.pdf |title=IEEE Standard for Local and metropolitan area networks--Part 15.4: Low-Rate Wireless Personal Area Networks (LR-WPANs) |date=2011-09-05 |chapter=Annex B: CCM* mode of operation|publisher=[[IEEE Standards]] |access-date=2015-12-18 |page=229}}</ref>

==Performance==

CCM requires two block cipher encryption operations on each block of an encrypted-and-authenticated message, and one encryption on each block of associated authenticated data.

According to [[Crypto++]] benchmarks, AES CCM requires 28.6 [[cycles per byte]] on an [[Intel Core 2|Intel Core 2 processor]] in 32-bit mode.<ref>{{cite web|title=Crypto++ 5.6.0 Benchmarks|url=http://www.cryptopp.com/benchmarks.html|website=Crypto++|access-date=6 September 2015}}</ref>

Notable inefficiencies:
* CCM is not an "on-line" [[Authenticated encryption#Authenticated_encryption_with_associated_data|authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD)]], in that the length of the message (and associated data) must be known in advance.
* In the MAC construction, the length of the associated data has a variable-length encoding, which can be shorter than machine word size.  This can cause pessimistic MAC performance if associated data is long (which is uncommon).
* Associated data is processed after message data, so it is not possible to pre-calculate state for static associated data.

==Patents==

The catalyst for the development of CCM mode was the submission of [[OCB mode|offset codebook (OCB) mode]] for inclusion in the [[IEEE 802.11i]] standard. Opposition was voiced to the inclusion of OCB mode because of a pending [[patent]] application on the [[algorithm]]. Inclusion of a patented algorithm meant significant licensing complications for implementors of the standard.

While the inclusion of OCB mode was disputed based on these [[intellectual property]] issues, it was agreed that the simplification provided by an authenticated encryption system was desirable.  Therefore, Housley, et al. developed CCM mode as a potential alternative that was not encumbered by patents.

Even though CCM mode is less efficient than OCB mode, a patent free solution was preferable to one complicated by patent licensing issues. Therefore, CCM mode went on to become a mandatory component of the IEEE 802.11i standard, and OCB mode was relegated to optional component status, before eventually being removed altogether.

==Use==
CCM mode is used in [[IEEE 802.11i]] (as [[CCMP (cryptography)|CCMP]], the CCM encryption protocol for [[WPA2]]), [[IPsec]],<ref>{{IETF RFC|4309}} Using Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) CCM Mode with IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)</ref> and [[Transport Layer Security|TLS]] 1.2,<ref>{{IETF RFC|6655}} AES-CCM Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)</ref> as well as [[Bluetooth Low Energy]] (as of [[Bluetooth#Bluetooth 4.0|Bluetooth 4.0]]).<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.bluetooth.com/~/media/files/specification/bluetooth-low-energy-security.ashx?la=en |title=Bluetooth Low Energy Security |access-date=2017-04-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160402235955/https://www.bluetooth.com/~/media/files/specification/bluetooth-low-energy-security.ashx?la=en |archive-date=2016-04-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref>It is available for TLS 1.3, but not enabled by default in [[OpenSSL]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://openssl-library.org/post/2017-05-04-tlsv1.3/ |title=Using TLS1.3 With OpenSSL |first=Matt |last=Caswell |date=2017-05-04 |access-date=2024-10-11 |publisher=[[OpenSSL]] blog}}</ref> From version 0.8<ref>{{Cite web |last=openzfs |title=Release zfs-0.8.0 · openzfs/zfs |url=https://github.com/openzfs/zfs/releases/tag/zfs-0.8.0 |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=GitHub |language=en}}</ref> to 0.8.3 it was the default in OpenZFS' native encryption<ref>{{Cite web |last=openzfs |title=ICP: Improve AES-GCM performance · openzfs/zfs@31b160f |url=https://github.com/openzfs/zfs/commit/31b160f0a6c673c8f926233af2ed6d5354808393 |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=GitHub |language=en}}</ref>.
